title: Only with a teacher
hookLine: both Mahamudra and Dzogchen are traditionally learned face to face

cards: Two people stop on a woodland path. One whispers: there's an owl. The other looks.
Bark, branches, leaves, more bark. Nothing. The first steps behind, lines up a finger beside the other's cheek, and points.
Third branch up. Where it forks. That gray lump.
And all at once the lump has eyes and a face, and it can't be unseen. A field guide could have described that owl for a year. It took a person, a finger and a moment, side by side.

teach.h: A TEACHER POINTS OUT THE MIND.
teach.b: First, the pointing out. Both Mahamudra and Dzogchen speak of a moment when a teacher points out the nature of the student's own mind.
Yesterday's first statement of Garab Dorje was: be introduced directly to your own nature. An introduction needs someone to make it.

The mind's nature, Tibetan teachers explain, is so close and so simple that we look straight past it, the way an eye can't see itself. Second, a story the Kagyu tell, which you first met in year three.

Naropa was a great scholar, tradition says, honored for his learning. Then he met the wild teacher Tilopa, who for years put him through hardship after hardship and taught him almost nothing in words.
In the story, the moment finally came when Tilopa struck him with a sandal, and Naropa saw. What a lifetime of reading had circled around, one face-to-face moment opened. Third, care on both sides.
The guru yoga lesson met the advice to examine a teacher.
Here it runs both ways: Tibetan texts on teacher and student advise each to examine the other before the relationship begins.

teach.h: SOME THINGS PASS ONLY IN PERSON.
teach.b: A pointing out only means something from a teacher whose own life shows the teaching.
Fourth, what's left for everyone else. Books, recordings and lessons like this one can describe these teachings and prepare the ground. Teachers in both lineages say the rest happens in person.
Saying so plainly is part of honoring the teaching.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism, Mahamudra and Dzogchen are traditionally received from a qualified teacher, often after preliminary practices, in a pointing-out instruction given in person; teacher and student are advised to examine each other before the relationship begins.

games.q: what does “only with a teacher” mean?
o: a rule that only monks may ever read the scriptures
a belief that books about Buddhism are forbidden
deep teachings passed in person, by a trusted teacher

games.q: face to face: tap the pairs.
p: a teacher shows the mind's nature

s: a book can do the pointing out as well as a teacher
books prepare the ground; the pointing out is traditionally given face to face.
in the story, Naropa's moment came through a face-to-face act, not a book
after years of hardship, Tilopa struck him with a sandal, and Naropa saw.
Tibetan teachers say the mind's nature is hard to see because it is so close
we look straight past it, the way an eye can't see itself.

games.q: you're Naropa: honored for your learning, and you've read everything. Tilopa still hasn't explained a thing in words. what opens it, in the story?
o: one more book, read more carefully.
a face-to-face moment with his teacher.
games.why: in the story, Tilopa strikes him with a sandal, and Naropa sees. what a lifetime of reading circled around, one moment in person opened.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you only learned because someone showed you, side by side: tying a shoe, riding a bike, a prayer, a recipe, how to be kind to someone who's grieving.
See their hands, their face, the moment it clicked, and let some thanks go toward them, wherever they are now.

wordCard.voice: Only with a teacher. In Tibetan tradition, Mahamudra and Dzogchen are learned face to face, when a trusted teacher points out the nature of the student's mind. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: face to face. Some things need a finger beside your cheek, not another page. Until tomorrow.
